reasons.realCost: WooCommerce itself is free, but the real monthly bill comes entirely from third-party hosting (Woo's own estimate: $25-$350/month) and yearly extensions, both of which vary by the buyer's own choices rather than a vendor price list.
reasons.pricingHonesty: WooCommerce's pricing page discloses the plugin is free with 0% revenue share, states its hosting-cost range and lists the full WooPayments fee schedule, though its own cost calculator emails results only after a lead-form submission.
reasons.smallTeamFit: Running WooCommerce means choosing and configuring a WordPress host, installing and maintaining plugins, and relying on community forums for free-core support, which typically calls for developer or agency help.
reasons.doesTheJob: The free core gives unlimited products, orders and APIs, and a large extension marketplace adds subscriptions, bookings and bundles, but each of those capabilities is a separate paid add-on rather than built in.
reasons.freedomToLeave: Because it is open-source code on self-hosted WordPress, an owner can move to any host or payment gateway at any time, and paid extensions keep working (minus updates and support) if a subscription lapses.
reasons.trackRecord: WooCommerce launched in 2011 and has been owned by Automattic since 2015, and it remains one of the most widely deployed ecommerce plugins for WordPress.

basis: WooCommerce is a good buy for a small business willing to manage, or pay someone to manage, WordPress hosting and plugins: its 0% platform fee and full code ownership are strong, but the total monthly cost is spread across a host and extensions the vendor doesn't set, and it offers no path to run without ongoing technical upkeep.
method: Two independent blind passes scored six factors (1–5) and an overall; published overall is the mean of the two overall scores, rounded down. Pass scores: 3.6 and 3.7.
